text:
If you've ever added a fallback so a rare failure wouldn't hurt anyone, go and check what fraction of your traffic is taking it.

Mine was taking all of it.

A verification widget sits in front of my sign-up. Widgets can be slow or blocked, so I wrote: wait six seconds, and if it hasn't answered by then, let the visitor through anyway.

The widget answers in eight and a half seconds.

The fallback was the only path, and it had been for five weeks. Zero new users for thirty-five days. None of them knew, and neither did I, because I'd built the emergency path to be silent.

A rare hiccup that happens every time stops being a hiccup and becomes the product.

Every founder has one of these. The pricing exception you'll make if the deal is good enough. The manual workaround for when the automation fails. Each is built for the rare case, each is easier than the thing it backs up, and none of them tells you how often it fires.

Whatever your fallback is, make it say so when it fires.

text:
For thirty-five days my sign-up flow rejected everybody. A real fault, mine, and I fixed it. The door opened at 10:15 on Monday morning.

Thirty-three hours later I ran the numbers. New sign-ups from people who are not me or my own test account: zero.

Nobody was standing outside.

For five weeks I'd had an excellent answer to why nothing was moving. The door was shut. Anybody would have been stuck. It was the kind of explanation that survives any question, because it's true. Then the door opened, the number stayed at zero, and the explanation went with it.

A broken door is fixable by someone with my skills. I can read a log, find a cause, ship a change, watch a status go green. Every minute of that feels like the job. Getting a stranger to care enough to arrive has no log to read.

So when a genuine technical fault appears it gets my full attention, and the harder problem waits. Not because I decided it should. Because one of them tells me when I'm done.

After you fix the thing you're certain is the problem, write down the number you expect to move and the date you'll check it.

text:
If you talk about your users as though you could reach them, run the query I ran this week. It took about a minute and it was not a good minute.

My database has sixty-nine users. There's a column on that table called consent_market, because we built the signup flow properly: explicit opt-in, plainly worded, no pre-ticked box.

One of them is true. Sixty-eight said no.

I'd been describing sixty-nine people as an audience. I have one person I can send an email to.

Nothing here is broken. Nobody made a mistake. The consent design did exactly what it was built to do, and I'd build it the same way again.

A bug you can fix. A number that's correct, honest and much smaller than the one in your head is a different problem. It doesn't announce itself.

Users are people who turned up and did something. A list is people you're permitted to contact. Mine were sixty-nine and one.

A signup feels like permission, which is worse than nothing, because it stops you looking.

Run the actual query. If your product has no such field, that is the finding.

text:
For most of my career, one sign told me a project was going well: the documentation.

If the key governance documents were written on time and approved by senior management, the project was usually in good shape. If they weren't getting done or weren't getting approved, that was a red flag, often weeks before the problem showed up in the budget or the schedule.

But a date alone wasn't enough. A document can be approved on time without anyone seriously questioning it.

So when I was drafting, I'd take each document to the senior managers one by one and have them tell me where they had difficulty with it. We'd resolve it at the time, with the general manager. Those discussions changed the document. Their concerns were addressed, and their wording often went into the text.

The credit belongs to the managers who gave the time. Reading a draft properly and arguing with it is work.

If you're reviewing a project, look at whose words are in the approved version.

It's very hard not to approve a document when your own words are in it.

text:
Before one project was formally approved, a colleague who knew the system and I spent more than six weeks reviewing every point where the public met the organisation, and what would have to change behind each one.

The most important document we produced came before the business case. It was the impact document.

It set out three options – the minimum, the middle and the full – and the assumptions behind each. The business case used it to set out the investment decision. The design drew on it, and was complete enough that the programmers used it as their specification. So did the testing.

The people who approved, built and tested the system all worked from that one piece of work.

No methodology asked for those six weeks. We spent them finding out what would have to change.

text:
Admitting you wrote a complete design document can sound like a confession these days. Agile is supposed to have settled that.

The Agile Manifesto (2001) values "Working software over comprehensive documentation". It also says, "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more".

Documents still had value. Working software came first.

And the Manifesto wasn't written to answer the question that comes first: should the organisation spend the money at all? SAFe calls for a lean business case for large initiatives. PRINCE2 Agile keeps continued business justification as a principle.

Agile changed how teams could learn during delivery. It didn't remove the need to learn before committing the organisation's money.

text:
Early in my career, in the mid-1980s, I worked for the Chief of Air Force Materiel in Canberra, where the Air Force's major and minor projects were managed.

The project management method was called Spectrum. It took up two shelves of a bookcase, in green binders.

They mostly sat on the shelf.

I wasn't a project officer on the major projects, so I can't say how well it was enforced. The organisation was changing, and I suspect Spectrum belonged to an earlier way of managing projects. It remained the formal doctrine. I couldn't tell from those binders how much of it was still practised.

A method can remain formally current without telling you how projects are being managed.

When an organisation changes, how does it know whether its project management standards still describe the way projects are actually run?

text:
When I was in the Air Force in Canberra, there was a famous project called the Supply Systems Redevelopment Project, the SSRP. It was Defence's attempt to put the supply systems of the Army, Navy and Air Force onto one common system.

I remember going into the Cameron Offices. The analysis was metres and metres of data mapping, up on the windows.

In 1990 the Canberra Times put the job at more than 1.5 million line items, worth over $5 billion. One steel washer had been found recorded more than a hundred times across the separate systems. Before three systems could become one, someone had to agree what each record meant.

The studies began in the mid-1970s. By July 1990, some of the team had taken to calling it the Tricentennial Project.

text:
Paper is cheap while each draft settles a question.

I've argued for iterating on paper first, because drafts cost less than delivery. The SSRP, Defence's long-running supply systems project, shows what that argument depends on. When an early decision or the politics keeps reopening the questions, the paper becomes the expense: years of salaries, offices and computers.

The people doing the work did eventually replace most of the old supply systems. Defence had a hard problem, and it would be wrong to call the whole undertaking a failure.

But delivery doesn't tell you whether the earlier years were well spent. Some analysis goes on because the problem is hard. Some goes on because the organisation can't agree on a decision.

Is each round of analysis closing a question, or opening the next one?

However many metres of paper went up on the windows, only the decisions told you whether the project was moving.
